name: Moringa

card.summary: A tropical tree whose seed oil and leaf extract show up in skin products, with antioxidant lab data but no skin-appearance trials.
card.note: Evidence is lab-based; oral safety data are limited.

quick.overview:
Moringa is a tree grown across the tropics. In skin care its seed oil and leaf extracts appear in moisturisers and body oils, marketed for moisturising and antioxidant effects.

Laboratory studies show leaf extracts have antioxidant activity, but no human trial found tests it for skin appearance.
quick.mechanism: Proposed benefits rest on its fatty-acid-rich oil acting as an emollient and on phenolic compounds such as quercetin and kaempferol that show antioxidant activity in the lab.
quick.risks: Topical products are generally labelled for external use. Oral use has limited human toxicity data and possible drug-metabolism interactions per Wikipedia, and Australia and New Zealand declined novel-food approval in 2025.

lead: Moringa usually refers to Moringa oleifera, a fast-growing, drought-resistant tree native to northern India and cultivated across the tropics, also called the drumstick, horseradish or ben tree and, in the Philippines, malunggay.[1] Its leaves, pods, flowers and seeds are eaten, and its seed oil (ben oil) is used in cosmetics and in skin- and hair-care products.[1]

The appearance angle is mainly topical and nutritional. In skin care, moringa seed oil and leaf extracts appear in creams, body oils and similar products marketed for moisturising or antioxidant benefits.[1][11] Leaf extracts show antioxidant activity in laboratory work, and a review of herbal creams loaded with plant extracts for protection against UV-driven oxidative damage lists Moringa oleifera among the botanicals studied.[4][5] Taken by mouth, leaf powder is sold as a greens supplement, and users describe it as an energy and nutrition source.[6]

Wikipedia states that despite considerable preliminary research, no high-quality evidence has been found that moringa affects health or disease.[1] No clinical trial found in the registries searched tests moringa for skin appearance; published human trials examine blood sugar, blood pressure and nutrition.[7][9][15]

chain: Seed oil or leaf extract is applied in a cream or body oil
Oil acts as an emollient and extracts add antioxidant compounds
Skin is moisturised and protected, as the products claim
angle.text: Moringa appears as a plant-oil and antioxidant ingredient in topical products. People use it for moisturised-looking skin and hair, and as a nutrient-dense leaf powder for general wellbeing.

paras: Moringa oleifera is a tree reaching roughly 10 to 12 metres with feathery tripinnate leaves, fragrant flowers and long three-sided pods.[1] The genus name comes from a Tamil word meaning twisted pod, and the species name refers to its oil.[1] Mature seeds yield about 38 to 40 percent oil, high in behenic acid and resistant to rancidity.[1]

Reviews describe the leaves as containing minerals, protein, vitamins, beta-carotene, amino acids and phenolic compounds such as quercetin and kaempferol, and Wikipedia lists notable vitamin C, B vitamins, provitamin A, vitamin K and manganese; the leaves also contain oxalates at levels comparable to spinach.[1][2][3] A 2023 review counted more than one hundred compounds characterised across the plant, including alkaloids, flavonoids, vitamins, glycosides and terpenes.[10]
Food. Pods are common in South Asian curries, leaves go into soups and are dried to powder, and flowers, seeds and roots are also eaten.[1] India is the largest producer.[1]

Oil and cosmetics. Wikipedia notes that moringa seed oil is used in food supplements and in cosmetics and can serve as a base for hair and skin care.[1] A US over-the-counter product listing shows moringa seed oil as one ingredient in a topical body oil sold for stretch marks, alongside sunflower, baobab, cocoa, echium and sesame ingredients, with labelling for external use only.[11] Such listings describe marketing claims rather than demonstrated effects.

Other uses. Moringa is used for honey production, livestock forage and nutrition programmes; seed proteins clump particles in turbid water, which has led to water-purification research, and leaf powder performed similarly to soap in one hand-washing study.[1]

sections.h: Use in skin and hair care
paras: Moringa products are marketed for moisturising and antioxidant effects. The rationale usually offered is that the fatty-acid-rich oil acts as an emollient and that leaf phenolics scavenge free radicals. Leaf extracts prepared with different solvents from three regions scavenged peroxyl and superoxide radicals in a 2003 laboratory study, and a 2015 review of antioxidant herbal creams includes moringa among botanicals studied for protection against UV-related oxidative stress.[4][5]
Published review literature describes the plant mainly in terms of nutrition and general medicinal use rather than controlled evidence for facial appearance.[3][10]

sections.h: Use in lifting and supplement communities
paras: Moringa appears only incidentally in forums. On T Nation, one member opened a thread on moringa as a nutrient-rich food and said they were thinking of trying it; another said a moringa product 'gave me nice energy and tasted like matcha without caffeine'; and a physique competitor listed maca and moringa among supplements in a diet post. Others mention growing it or cooking it in a Filipino chicken stew.[6][12][13][14]

No human studies on moringa for skin appearance were found. Registered and published human trials have looked at other uses, including leaf extract in rheumatoid arthritis, leaf intake in prediabetes and metabolic syndrome, leaf extract and exercise performance in young men, postprandial blood pressure, and moringa toothpastes and varnishes in oral health.[7][8][9][15][16][17] A 2015 safety and efficacy review reported that five human studies of powdered whole leaf had shown anti-hyperglycaemic and anti-dyslipidaemic activities and that no adverse effects were reported in human studies, while noting that product standardisation is an issue.[18] A systematic review and meta-analysis has examined moringa in diabetes mellitus.[19]
Laboratory work has measured the antioxidant capacity of leaf extracts from different regions and at different maturity stages.[4][20]

Wikipedia reports that human toxicity data are limited, that leaf extract is considered potentially toxic above 3,000 mg/kg body weight, that moringa may interact with cytochrome P450 drug metabolism, and that in November 2025 Food Standards Australia New Zealand rejected an application to approve moringa leaves, immature pods and oil as a novel food, citing insufficient safety evidence.[1] These points concern ingestion rather than topical cosmetic use.

In September 2026 Foods Alive Inc. recalled its organic moringa leaf powder in the US over possible Salmonella contamination, traced to a supplier's green powder mix; the company reported no illnesses.[21]

timeline.event: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck formally describes Moringa oleifera.[1]
Laboratory study measures antioxidant activity of moringa leaf extracts from three regions.[4]
Phytotherapy Research review describes moringa as a food plant with multiple medicinal uses.[2]
Reviews of leaf pharmacology and of safety and efficacy; review of antioxidant herbal creams includes moringa.[3][18][5]
Randomized trial of leaf supplementation in prediabetes.[15]
Australia and New Zealand reject a novel-food application for moringa leaves, pods and oil.[1]
US recall of an organic moringa leaf powder over possible Salmonella.[21]
